title: Evidence-Based 4-Day Hypertrophy (PPLA)
author: Bradley
desc:
This program is engineered for one objective: skeletal muscle hypertrophy — an increase in muscle fiber cross-sectional area via mechanical tension, adequate weekly volume, and proximity to muscular failure. It is not a strength, powerbuilding, or fat-loss template.

Structure. Four days per week organized as Push, Pull, Legs, and Accessory. Every major muscle receives two weekly exposures — the frequency most consistently supported by the hypertrophy literature — with additional Day 4 volume allocated to the musculature with the greatest influence on upper-body visual proportion: lateral deltoid, clavicular pectoralis, latissimus dorsi, biceps, and triceps. Sessions may be performed on any four days that accommodate the trainee's schedule.

Volume. Weekly working-set volume targets 10–20 hard sets per muscle group, scaled to trainee tolerance.

Intensity (RPE). RPE 8 = 2 reps in reserve; RPE 9 = 1 RIR; RPE 10 = momentary muscular failure. Compound movements are generally capped at RPE 9 to manage joint and systemic fatigue; isolation movements and final sets of compounds, where failure is safe, are taken to RPE 9–10. Where two RPE values are dashed in the prescription (e.g. "8–9"), early sets are performed at the lower bound and the final set at the upper bound, producing a brief intra-exercise effort ramp.

Rep ranges. Current evidence demonstrates statistically equivalent hypertrophy across rep ranges from approximately 5 to 30 when effort is equated. Ranges are therefore assigned by mechanical fit: compounds in the 6–12 range (optimal tension-to-fatigue ratio) and isolations in the 10–20 range (where stability ceases to be the limiting factor at near-failure loads).

Progressive overload. Double progression. At the current load, add repetitions within the prescribed range session over session; once the top of the range is cleared on all working sets at the target RPE, increase load by the smallest available increment and re-enter the range from the bottom. Tempo, range of motion, and execution standard are held constant so that load progression reflects genuine contractile improvement.

Execution. Eccentric phases are controlled across 2–3 seconds; concentric phases are executed with intent but without ballistic acceleration. Full range of motion on every repetition. Rest 2–3 minutes between compound sets and 60–90 seconds between isolation sets. All working sets are logged to enable week-over-week comparison and targeted overload.

Exercise selection. Every primary movement is a standard commercial-gym staple. Each prescribed alternate reproduces the primary exercise's stimulus on equipment universally available, using identical sets, rep range, and RPE targets. Alternates resolve equipment contention, not secondary training effects.

Scope. The program prescribes resistance training only. Nutrition, sleep, cardio, and mesocycle-level periodization (deload timing, block-to-block volume progression) remain the trainee's responsibility.

ex.note: Retract and depress scapulae, 2-second eccentric, bar to lower chest, no bounce. Primary horizontal pressing compound for pectoral cross-sectional area.
Bench at ~30°. Lower dumbbells to shoulder level with full stretch; do not lock out in order to maintain continuous tension on the clavicular pectoralis.
Slight back incline (~10°) is acceptable. Stop short of full elbow lockout to preserve tension on the anterior deltoid and reduce joint load.
Low-pulley cable run across the body, slight forward torso lean, lead with the elbow. The lateral deltoid is a primary driver of shoulder width and upper-body visual taper.
Overhead position places the triceps long head — the largest of the three heads — under maximal stretch, which is the most hypertrophy-productive joint position.
Elbows fixed at the sides, full elbow extension at the bottom with a brief peak contraction. Pairs with overhead work to cover both ends of the triceps length–tension curve.
Posteriorly tilt the pelvis at the top rather than swinging the legs. Progress by holding a dumbbell between the feet or adding ankle weights once the top of the rep range is reached.
Full dead hang, drive elbows down and back toward the hips, controlled 2–3 second eccentric, no kipping. Primary vertical pulling stimulus for lat width.
Torso at ~45°, neutral spine, pull bar to the lower sternum. Primary loaded horizontal pull for thickness across the mid-traps, rhomboids, and lats.
Drive elbows toward hip pockets, peak contraction for one count, allow a full scapular protraction in the stretch position without lumbar flexion.
Elbows above shoulder level, external rotation through the full range. Targets the posterior deltoid and scapular upward-rotators, which round out shoulder development visually.
Arms positioned behind the torso place the biceps long head under stretch, biasing the peak. Full range, 2-second eccentric, no swinging.
Upper arm fixed against the pad eliminates momentum and isolates the biceps at a shortened position, complementing Incline Curl’s stretch bias for full length–tension coverage.
Focus on rib-cage-to-pelvis spinal flexion rather than hip flexion. Load is the primary progression variable — add weight when the top of the rep range is cleared on all sets.
Full depth with hips descending below the knee, feet shoulder-width, heels down. Substitutes for back-squat loading patterns while minimizing axial spinal load.
Hips back, soft knees, bar tracked against the thighs, 2–3 second eccentric. Terminate each rep at the onset of lumbar flexion or loss of hamstring tension.
Rear foot elevated, front shin near vertical for glute bias. Unilateral loading addresses bilateral asymmetries that bilateral lifts systematically mask.
1-second peak contraction, controlled eccentric. Quadriceps isolation on a fixed path is the safest environment to train to true muscular failure on the final set.
Seated position places the hamstrings on stretch at the hip, a more hypertrophy-productive length than the lying variation. Pause one count at peak contraction each rep.
Full stretch at the bottom with a one-count pause, full plantarflexion at the top. Gastrocnemius responds to high intensity; train each set to genuine failure.
Hold a plate against the chest. Decline increases range of motion compared to flat crunches. Rotate with Day 2’s Cable Crunch to vary ab loading vectors across the week.
Second weekly exposure of incline pressing. Treat as a hypertrophy-focused session with a slightly lighter load and longer time under tension than Day 1’s pressing block.
Torso fully supported removes the lower back as a limiter, allowing the upper back and lats to be trained closer to concentric failure than a free-standing row permits.
Second weekly exposure of lateral-deltoid work. Frequency and volume on this muscle are the primary levers for shoulder-width development; program both sessions deliberately.
Isolates the posterior deltoid with minimal scapular retraction, complementing Day 2’s Face Pull. Full stretch in the bottom position, one-count peak contraction at the top.
Stable, loadable straight-arm curl pattern. EZ-bar wrist angle reduces forearm stress. Prioritize clean progressive overload here; this is the primary mass-driver for biceps.
Lower the bar behind the head rather than to the forehead to bias the long head via full stretch. Complements Day 1’s standing overhead extension as a supine stretch variant.
Anti-extension loading: brace the abdominal wall throughout, never allow lumbar extension. Progress by rolling further, then from knees to standing over many weeks.
